sources.title: Emily Riehl, Category Theory in Context
sources.locator: Chapter 2, complete section and named-result harvest of §§2.1–2.4 (printed pp. 54–80): §2.1 Representable functors, §2.2 The Yoneda lemma, §2.3 Universal properties and universal elements, and §2.4 The category of elements; exercises are outside the named-result harvest

contents.name: Section 2.1, Representable functors
Example 2.1.1, the natural numbers with successor and zero as the universal discrete dynamical system
contents.reason: This is a categorical reformulation of the recursion theorem for natural numbers; it is not used by the retained representability or Yoneda development.

contents.name: Definition 2.1.3, initial and terminal objects characterized by representability of the terminal Set-valued functor
Definition 2.1.4, a representation and a representable functor
Example 2.1.5(i), the identity functor on Set represented by a singleton
Example 2.1.5(ii), the underlying-set functor on Top represented by the one-point space
Example 2.1.5(iii), the underlying-set functor on groups represented by the infinite cyclic group
Example 2.1.5(iv), the underlying-set functor on left R-modules represented by the regular module R
contents.reason: The one-generator free-module representation belongs with the planned tensor-products-of-modules development; no retained Yoneda result depends on this module-specific instance.

contents.name: Example 2.1.5(v), the underlying-set functor on unital rings represented by Z[x]
Example 2.1.5(vi), n-tuples in groups represented by the free group on n generators
Example 2.1.5(vi), n-tuples in abelian groups represented by the free abelian group on n generators
contents.reason: The abelian-group variant requires the free-module-over-Z construction and belongs with module theory rather than this category-theory pair.

contents.name: Example 2.1.5(vii), tuples satisfying relations represented by the group carrying the corresponding presentation
contents.reason: This application belongs to the published free-groups-and-presentations topic; the present pair neither needs nor redevelops presentation realizations.

contents.name: Example 2.1.5(viii), the units functor on unital rings represented by Z[x,x^{-1}]
contents.reason: A proof needs Laurent-polynomial or localization machinery not present in this pair, and the units representation is not used by any retained item.

contents.name: Example 2.1.5(ix), the object functor on small categories represented by the terminal category
contents.reason: This Cat-valued worked representation is independent of the retained walking-arrow Yoneda computation and is not needed in an A-page proof.

contents.name: Example 2.1.5(x), the morphism functor on small categories represented by the walking-arrow category
contents.reason: The B page computes the Yoneda embedding inside the walking-arrow category, not the distinct functor Cat(2,-) on all small categories.

contents.name: Example 2.1.5(xi), the isomorphism functor on small categories represented by the walking-isomorphism category
contents.reason: The walking-isomorphism classifier is a separate finite-category example and supplies no machinery used in this page's Yoneda or universality proofs.

contents.name: Example 2.1.5(xii), composable n-paths represented by the ordinal category n+1
contents.reason: This family of walking-path classifiers would require a separate finite-category computation and is not needed by any retained dependency route.

contents.name: Example 2.1.5(xiii), the underlying-set functor on pointed sets represented by a two-element pointed set
contents.reason: Pointed-set classifiers are a separate concrete-category example; the current pair already retains Set, Top, group, monoid, ring, and poset computations.

contents.name: Example 2.1.5(xiv), path and loop functors represented by the interval and the circle
contents.reason: This representation requires the topology and homotopy conventions for path spaces and loops, none of which is load-bearing for the present page.

contents.name: Example 2.1.6(i), the contravariant power-set functor represented by a two-element classifier
contents.reason: The subobject-classifier example is not required by the retained representability theorems and would add a separate power-set construction to the companion.

contents.name: Example 2.1.6(ii), the open-subset functor on Top represented by the Sierpinski space
contents.reason: The published topology example proves inverse-image functoriality, but not this Sierpinski representation; the latter is not used by the current proofs.

contents.name: Example 2.1.6(iii), the closed-subset functor represented by the Sierpinski space and naturally isomorphic to the open-subset functor
contents.reason: Complement naturality is already published, but the additional Sierpinski representability claim would need its own topology example and is not used here.

contents.name: Example 2.1.6(iv), the functor Hom(- × A, B) represented by the exponential B^A
Example 2.1.6(v), the dual-vector underlying-set presheaf represented by the ground field
contents.reason: This linear-algebra instance belongs with dual vector spaces and is not needed to establish the general contravariant representability machinery.

contents.name: Example 2.1.6(vi), singular cohomology represented by Eilenberg-Mac Lane spaces on the CW homotopy category
contents.reason: The claim depends on singular cohomology, CW complexes, homotopy categories, and Eilenberg-Mac Lane spaces far beyond this pair's prerequisites.

contents.name: Example 2.1.6(vii), principal G-bundles represented by a classifying space BG
contents.reason: Classifying spaces and principal bundles require an algebraic-topology track not available to this category-theory page and are not used downstream here.

contents.name: Section 2.2, The Yoneda lemma
Example 2.2.1, represented omega-diagrams and natural transformations determined at the representing index
contents.reason: This ordinal-diagram computation is an optional specialized example and is not used in the proof of the general evaluation bijection.

contents.name: Example 2.2.2, representable functors on a one-object group category as regular actions
Proposition 2.2.3, equivariant maps from the regular G-set to X correspond to elements of X
Theorem 2.2.4, the Yoneda lemma with its evaluation map, inverse formula, and naturality in both variables
Remark 2.2.7, evaluation represents the natural-transformation assignment for a small source and the size caveat for a large source
Corollary 2.2.8, the covariant and contravariant Yoneda embeddings are fully faithful
Example 2.2.9, natural transformations between the object and morphism functors on Cat classified by maps between 1 and 2
contents.reason: This requires first scaffolding the distinct Cat-wide object and morphism representations declined above; it is not needed by the retained Yoneda consequences.

contents.name: Corollary 2.2.10, every row operation is left multiplication by the matrix obtained by applying it to the identity
contents.reason: The published disk theorem covers only the three elementary row operations, whereas Riehl's corollary classifies arbitrary natural row operations; those are not the same statement.

contents.name: Corollary 2.2.11, Cayley's theorem
Section 2.3, Universal properties and universal elements
Proposition 2.3.1, objects are isomorphic exactly when their represented hom-functors are naturally isomorphic
Corollary 2.3.2, representing objects are unique up to a compatible isomorphism
Definition 2.3.3, universal elements
Example 2.3.4, x in Z[x] as the universal element for the underlying-set functor on unital rings
Example 2.3.6, the singleton subset {top} as the universal element of the contravariant power-set functor
contents.reason: This universal-element computation depends on the power-set classifier representation declined at Example 2.1.6(i), and no retained item uses it.

contents.name: Example 2.3.7, representable G-sets as torsors and a chosen origin as universal element
contents.reason: The torsor criterion is a group-action application beyond the monoid evaluation example and is not a prerequisite for the page's general Yoneda machinery.

contents.name: Example 2.3.8, tensor products representing bilinear maps via a universal bilinear element
contents.reason: The tensor-product representation belongs to the planned tensor-products-of-modules page, whose construction and bilinear universal property are not rebuilt here.

contents.name: Proposition 2.3.10, symmetry of tensor products derived from the universal property
contents.reason: Tensor symmetry requires the tensor-product object and its bilinear universal property, so it belongs with the dedicated tensor-products-of-modules development.

contents.name: Remark 2.3.12, the swap isomorphism characterized by w tensor v mapping to v tensor w
contents.reason: This formula refines the deferred tensor-symmetry proposition and cannot be stated honestly before the tensor-product construction and notation are available.

contents.name: Example 2.3.13, the group ring Z[G] characterized by a universal property in unital rings
contents.reason: The group-ring construction and its units-compatible universal property belong to ring-extension theory and are not needed by the current category-theory pair.

contents.name: Section 2.4, The category of elements
Definition 2.4.1, category of elements of a covariant functor
Definition 2.4.2, category of elements of a contravariant functor
Example 2.4.3, the category of elements of n-Color as colored graphs and color-preserving graph homomorphisms
contents.reason: This graph-coloring instance needs the n-Color presheaf and graph-homomorphism conventions, none of which is used by the general category-of-elements theorem.

contents.name: Example 2.4.4, the category of elements of a concrete forgetful functor as pointed objects
contents.reason: The generic theory is retained, but this concrete-category specialization would duplicate pointed-object examples without contributing a new dependency route.

contents.name: Example 2.4.5, the category of elements of an indexed family over a discrete category as its dependent sum
contents.reason: Dependent sums and products are indexed-family or type-theoretic constructions and are not used by the categorical universal-property results retained here.

contents.name: Example 2.4.6, categories of elements of represented hom-functors are slice and coslice categories
Lemma 2.4.7, a presheaf category of elements as a comma category
Proposition 2.4.8, universal elements are initial or terminal objects in categories of elements
Proposition 2.4.9, the subcategory of representations is empty or a contractible groupoid
Example 2.4.10, the category of elements of a G-set as its action groupoid and representability as the torsor condition
contents.reason: The action-groupoid construction is already published, but the additional torsor representability criterion is a group-action application not used in this pair.

contents.name: Example 2.4.11, discrete dynamical systems as a category of elements with the natural numbers initial
contents.reason: This repeats the recursion-based natural-number example from 2.1.1 in category-of-elements form and is not used by any retained proof.

contents.name: Example 2.4.12(i), chosen subsets as a category of elements with the two-element classifier terminal
contents.reason: The computation depends on the declined power-set classifier example and adds no machinery required by the general terminal-object characterization.

contents.name: Example 2.4.12(ii), vectors with a chosen vector and the nonzero pointed one-dimensional spaces as initial objects
contents.reason: This vector-space classification belongs with free modules and duality examples; it is not required to prove the general category-of-elements equivalence.

contents.name: Example 2.4.12(iii), bilinear maps as a category of elements with the universal tensor map initial
contents.reason: This category-of-elements application depends on the tensor-product universal property and is deferred with that construction to tensor-products-of-modules.

contents.name: Example 2.4.12(iv), groups with n chosen elements and the free group on n generators as an initial object
Example 2.4.12(v), vector spaces with a dual vector as a slice category with identity on the ground field terminal
contents.reason: This uses dual-vector and slice computations specific to linear algebra and is not load-bearing for the general presheaf category-of-elements theorem.

contents.name: Example 2.4.12(vi), the underlying-set functor on unital rings represented by x in Z[x]
Definition 2.4.13, discrete left and right fibrations
contents.reason: Discrete fibration theory is a substantial extension of categories of elements and is not needed for their universal-element characterization on this page.

contents.name: Proposition 2.4.14, the category-of-elements construction is fully faithful with essential image the discrete left or right fibrations
contents.reason: This Grothendieck-construction theorem depends on the declined discrete-fibration machinery and is not used by any retained Yoneda or universal-arrow result.

sources.locator: Chapter 4, complete section and named-result harvest of §§4.1–4.3 (printed pp. 84–106): §4.1 Definitions and examples (pp. 84–92), §4.2 The Yoneda lemma (pp. 93–98), and §4.3 Consequences of the Yoneda lemma (pp. 99–106); exercises are outside the named-result harvest

contents.name: Section 4.1, Definitions and examples
Definition 4.1.1, the covariant hom-functor H_A
Remarks 4.1.2, local smallness for hom-sets and notation for postcomposition
Definition 4.1.3, covariant representability and a representation
Example 4.1.4, the identity functor on Set represented by a one-element set
Example 4.1.5, the underlying-set functor on Top represented by the one-point space
Example 4.1.5, the underlying-set functor on groups represented by the infinite cyclic group
Example 4.1.5, elements of order one or p represented by the cyclic group Z/pZ
contents.reason: This prime-order group classifier is a specialized cyclic-group example and is not needed by the monoid-action or general Yoneda arguments retained here.

contents.name: Example 4.1.6, the object functor on Cat represented by the terminal category
contents.reason: This is the Cat-wide object classifier rather than the retained finite Yoneda computation inside the walking-arrow category, so it has no dependency role here.

contents.name: Example 4.1.7, the unique representable functor on a one-object monoid category as the left regular action
Example 4.1.8, the underlying set of the fundamental group represented by the circle in the pointed homotopy category
contents.reason: Representability here uses pointed homotopy classes and the fundamental group of the circle, which lie outside this pair's category-theory prerequisites.

contents.name: Example 4.1.9, the bilinear-map functor represented by the tensor product
contents.reason: The tensor-product representation belongs to the planned tensor-products-of-modules page and is not assumed by any result retained in this pair.

contents.name: Lemma 4.1.10, an adjunction makes A(A,G(-)) representable by F(A)
contents.reason: This theorem depends on adjunctions and their natural hom-bijection, machinery assigned to the later adjunctions-and-the-adjoint-functor-theorems page.

contents.name: Proposition 4.1.11, every Set-valued functor with a left adjoint is representable
contents.reason: The proposition is a consequence of the adjunction lemma and belongs with the later adjunction page; the current page does not use it to prove representability.

contents.name: Example 4.1.12, the Top underlying-set and Cat object functors represented via their left adjoints
contents.reason: These examples use free or discrete left adjoints, so their advertised route belongs with adjunctions rather than the direct representations proved in this companion.

contents.name: Example 4.1.13, the underlying-set functor on vector spaces represented by the ground field
contents.reason: The one-generator free-vector-space representation belongs with the module and tensor-product development and is not needed by this page's general theorems.

contents.name: Example 4.1.14, the underlying-set functor on commutative rings represented by Z[x]
Definition 4.1.15, the family of covariant representables as a contravariant functor
Definition 4.1.16, the contravariant hom-functor H^A
Definition 4.1.17, contravariant representability and a representation
Example 4.1.18, the contravariant power-set functor represented by the two-element set
contents.reason: The power-set classifier is a separate Set example and is not required by any retained proof or by the companion's chosen finite computations.

contents.name: Example 4.1.19, the open-subset functor on Top represented by the Sierpinski space
contents.reason: The published topology item establishes inverse-image functoriality but not this representation; adding the Sierpinski classifier would be an independent example.

contents.name: Example 4.1.20, the underlying-set presheaf of continuous real-valued functions represented by the real line
contents.reason: This tautological Top(-,R) instance adds no new machinery beyond the definition of a representable presheaf and is not used by retained results.

contents.name: Definition 4.1.21, the Yoneda embedding
Definition 4.1.22, the hom-bifunctor
Remarks 4.1.23, the hom-bifunctor and its two curried families of hom-functors
Remark 4.1.24, the natural hom-bifunctor isomorphism formulation of an adjunction
contents.reason: This is a reformulation of adjunction data and belongs to adjunctions-and-the-adjoint-functor-theorems, whose machinery is later than this page.

contents.name: Definition 4.1.25, generalized elements and their shapes
Section 4.2, The Yoneda lemma
Theorem 4.2.1, the Yoneda lemma natural in both A and X
Section 4.3, Consequences of the Yoneda lemma
Notation 4.3.1, an arrow decorated with a tilde denotes an isomorphism
Subheading, A representation is a universal element
Corollary 4.3.2, a representation is a universal element and conversely
Corollary 4.3.3, the covariant dual characterization of representations by universal elements
Example 4.3.4, the free-vector-space representation expressed as its universal extension property
contents.reason: This concrete free-vector-space construction belongs with module theory; the current page proves the abstract equivalence without assuming that construction.

contents.name: Example 4.3.5, an adjunction represented by its unit as an initial comma-category object
contents.reason: The example requires an adjunction and its unit and is assigned to the later adjunctions-and-the-adjoint-functor-theorems development.

contents.name: Example 4.3.6, the two universal elements 1 and -1 for the underlying-set functor on groups
contents.reason: The companion retains the free-group representation itself; classifying its two choices of generator is an additional automorphism-counting example not used elsewhere.

contents.name: Subheading, The Yoneda embedding
Corollary 4.3.7, the Yoneda embedding is full and faithful
Lemma 4.3.8, full and faithful functors reflect isomorphisms and uniquely lift isomorphisms between image objects
Example 4.3.9, exactly two representations of the group underlying-set functor arising from the generators of Z
contents.reason: This refines the declined generator-counting Example 4.3.6 and is not needed for compatible uniqueness of arbitrary representing objects.

contents.name: Subheading, Isomorphism of representables
Corollary 4.3.10, objects are isomorphic exactly when their representable functors are isomorphic
Example 4.3.11, group objects compared through generalized elements of several shapes and naturally through all shapes
contents.reason: The all-shapes conclusion is retained abstractly, but this group-specific comparison needs cyclic-group computations not required by the page's proof.

contents.name: Example 4.3.12, ordinary elements of singleton shape suffice to determine a set
Example 4.3.13, uniqueness up to natural isomorphism of left or right adjoints to a fixed functor
contents.reason: This consequence requires the definition and naturality data of an adjunction, so it belongs with the later adjunction page rather than being assumed here.

contents.name: Example 4.3.14, uniqueness of a representing object illustrated by the tensor product
